Content:
Let [MATH: \mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j] be a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] and [MATH: C] be a closed curve in the [MATH: xy]-plane. Recall that the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] through [MATH: C] is given by the line integral

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.]

Content:
Calculating flux using this definition is often cumbersome because we need to calculate [MATH: \mathbf n,] the outward-pointing unit normal vector.

Content:
In practice, we often use the following alternative formula to calculate the flux:

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson.

Content:
Watch Out! When applying this formula, we must choose a positively-oriented parameterization for [MATH: C.] This formula will not work if [MATH: C] is negatively oriented!

items.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

key_prerequisites.name: Sums of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Parametric Curves

sections.normalized_html: Calculate the flux of the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = (y - x)\,\mathbf{i} - (x + y )\,\mathbf{j}] across the closed curve [MATH: C] given by [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}] for [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi).]
sections.readable_text: Calculate the flux of the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = (y - x)\,\mathbf{i} - (x + y )\,\mathbf{j}] across the closed curve [MATH: C] given by [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}] for [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j] is a vector field and [MATH: C] is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C] is given by [MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,] where [MATH: \mathbf{n}] denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to [MATH: C.]

Along the curve [MATH: C,] we have [MATH: x = 4\cos t, \qquad y = 4\sin t.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(x, y)|= y − x = 4(\sin t − \cos t),; Q(x, y)|= − (x + y) = − 4(\cos t + \sin t).]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x(t)] and [MATH: y(t)] along the curve, we get

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(4\cos t) = − 4\sin t,; (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(4\sin t) = 4\cos t.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

[MATH: ∮_(C)F ⋅ nds|= ∮_(C)Pdy − Qdx; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(P ⋅ (dy)/(dt) − Q ⋅ (dx)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(4(\sin t − \cos t)) ⋅ (4\cos t) − (− 4(\cos t + \sin t)) ⋅ (− 4\sin t)dt; = 16∫_{0}^{2π}\sin t\cos t − \cos^{2} t − \sin t\cos t − \sin^{2} tdt; = 16∫_{0}^{2π}(− 1)dt; = − 16t|_{0}^{2π}; = − 16(2π − 0); = − 32π]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j] is a vector field and [MATH: C] is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C] is given by [MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,] where [MATH: \mathbf{n}] denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to [MATH: C.]

First, we write the equation of our curve as

[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.]

The closed curve [MATH: C] is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes [MATH: 1] and [MATH: 3,] respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.]

Along the curve [MATH: C,] we have [MATH: x = \cos t, \qquad y = 3\sin t.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(x, y)|= xy = 3\sin t\cos t,; Q(x, y)|= x^{2} = \cos^{2} t.]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x(t)] and [MATH: y(t)] along the curve, we get

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(\cos t) = − \sin t,; (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(3\sin t) = 3\cos t.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution [MATH: u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,] as follows:

[MATH: ∮_(C)F ⋅ nds|= ∮_(C)Pdy − Qdx; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(P ⋅ (dy)/(dt) − Q ⋅ (dx)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(3\sin t\cos t) ⋅ (3\cos t) − (\cos^{2} t) ⋅ (− \sin t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}9\sin t\cos^{2} t + \sin t\cos^{2} tdt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}10\sin t\cos^{2} tdt; = − ∫_{1}^{1}10u^{2}du; = 0]

Content:
As we've seen, the flux of a vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] through a piecewise-smooth, closed curve [MATH: C] is a unique scalar number that represents the net flow of [MATH: \mathbf F] through [MATH: C.]

Content:
The question now is, does the notion of flux exist for curves that are not closed?

Content:
Indeed, it is possible to define the notion of flux through a non-closed curve. However, there is one crucial difference we need to bear in mind:

Content:
- In the case of a smooth, closed curve, it is always clear which direction is "out." Therefore, the outward-pointing unit normal vector [MATH: \mathbf n] is unique at every point on [MATH: C.]
- However, on a smooth, non-closed curve, there is no clear notion of "in" and "out." Instead, we can choose between two normal vectors at any point on the curve, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/6369cd4c1f33e340dfed5c9549faf388]

Content:
Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction.

Content:
For example, for the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] and curve [MATH: C] below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

[IMG: /graphics/c2b0b1dd1b411a746a1874d556157a62]

Content:
Finally, to calculate the flux of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] across a non-closed curve [MATH: C,] we can continue to use the formula

Content:

Content:
Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
First, recall that if [MATH: C] is parameterized by the function [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j] for [MATH: t\in [a,b],] then

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},]
where it is assumed that [MATH: C] is positively-oriented.

Content:
Substituting our expression for [MATH: \mathbf n] into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that [MATH: \textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,] we get

Content:
[MATH: ∮_(C)F ⋅ nds|= ∮_(C)(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ ((y^{′}(t)i − x^{′}(t)j)/(||r^{′}(t)||))||r^{′}(t)||dt; = ∮_(C)(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ ((y^{′}(t)i − x^{′}(t)j)/(||r^{′}(t)||))||r^{′}(t)||dt; = ∮_(C)(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ (y^{′}(t)i − x^{′}(t)j)dt; = ∮_(C)P(x(t), y(t))y^{′}(t) − Q(x(t), y(t))x^{′}(t)dt; = ∮_(C)Pdy − Qdx.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: \mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j] be a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] and [MATH: C] be a closed curve in the [MATH: xy]-plane. Recall that the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] through [MATH: C] is given by the line integral

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.]

Content:
Calculating flux using this definition is often cumbersome because we need to calculate [MATH: \mathbf n,] the outward-pointing unit normal vector.

Content:
In practice, we often use the following alternative formula to calculate the flux:

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson.

Content:
Watch Out! When applying this formula, we must choose a positively-oriented parameterization for [MATH: C.] This formula will not work if [MATH: C] is negatively oriented!

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

Example Prompt:
Calculate the flux of the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = (y - x)\,\mathbf{i} - (x + y )\,\mathbf{j}] across the closed curve [MATH: C] given by [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}] for [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j] is a vector field and [MATH: C] is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C] is given by
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,]
where [MATH: \mathbf{n}] denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to [MATH: C.]

Along the curve [MATH: C,] we have
[MATH: x = 4\cos t, \qquad
y = 4\sin t.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(x, y)|= y − x = 4(\sin t − \cos t),; Q(x, y)|= − (x + y) = − 4(\cos t + \sin t).]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x(t)] and [MATH: y(t)] along the curve, we get

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(4\cos t) = − 4\sin t,; (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(4\sin t) = 4\cos t.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

[MATH: ∮_(C)F ⋅ nds|= ∮_(C)Pdy − Qdx; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(P ⋅ (dy)/(dt) − Q ⋅ (dx)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(4(\sin t − \cos t)) ⋅ (4\cos t) − (− 4(\cos t + \sin t)) ⋅ (− 4\sin t)dt; = 16∫_{0}^{2π}\sin t\cos t − \cos^{2} t − \sin t\cos t − \sin^{2} tdt; = 16∫_{0}^{2π}(− 1)dt; = − 16t|_{0}^{2π}; = − 16(2π − 0); = − 32π]

---

Item 5 — Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

Example Prompt:
Calculate the flux of the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j}] across the ellipse [MATH: C] with equation [MATH: 9x^2 + y^2 = 9.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j] is a vector field and [MATH: C] is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C] is given by
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,]
where [MATH: \mathbf{n}] denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to [MATH: C.]

First, we write the equation of our curve as

[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.]

The closed curve [MATH: C] is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes [MATH: 1] and [MATH: 3,] respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.]

Along the curve [MATH: C,] we have
[MATH: x = \cos t, \qquad
y = 3\sin t.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(x, y)|= xy = 3\sin t\cos t,; Q(x, y)|= x^{2} = \cos^{2} t.]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x(t)] and [MATH: y(t)] along the curve, we get

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(\cos t) = − \sin t,; (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(3\sin t) = 3\cos t.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution [MATH: u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,] as follows:

[MATH: ∮_(C)F ⋅ nds|= ∮_(C)Pdy − Qdx; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(P ⋅ (dy)/(dt) − Q ⋅ (dx)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}(3\sin t\cos t) ⋅ (3\cos t) − (\cos^{2} t) ⋅ (− \sin t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}9\sin t\cos^{2} t + \sin t\cos^{2} tdt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}10\sin t\cos^{2} tdt; = − ∫_{1}^{1}10u^{2}du; = 0]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Calculating Flux for Non-Closed Curves

Content:
As we've seen, the flux of a vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] through a piecewise-smooth, closed curve [MATH: C] is a unique scalar number that represents the net flow of [MATH: \mathbf F] through [MATH: C.]

Content:
The question now is, does the notion of flux exist for curves that are not closed?

Content:
Indeed, it is possible to define the notion of flux through a non-closed curve. However, there is one crucial difference we need to bear in mind:

Content:
- In the case of a smooth, closed curve, it is always clear which direction is "out." Therefore, the outward-pointing unit normal vector [MATH: \mathbf n] is unique at every point on [MATH: C.]
- However, on a smooth, non-closed curve, there is no clear notion of "in" and "out." Instead, we can choose between two normal vectors at any point on the curve, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/6369cd4c1f33e340dfed5c9549faf388]

Content:
Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction.

Content:
For example, for the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] and curve [MATH: C] below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c2b0b1dd1b411a746a1874d556157a62]

Content:
Finally, to calculate the flux of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] across a non-closed curve [MATH: C,] we can continue to use the formula

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
Watch Out! To apply this formula, we usually need to parameterize [MATH: C.] It is vital that we pick a parameterization where the unit normal vector [MATH: \mathbf n] is a [MATH: 90^\circ] clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector [MATH: \mathbf T(t).]

---

Item 12 — Tutorial: Deriving the Main Formula

Content:
Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
First, recall that if [MATH: C] is parameterized by the function [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j] for [MATH: t\in [a,b],] then

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},]
where it is assumed that [MATH: C] is positively-oriented.

Content:
Substituting our expression for [MATH: \mathbf n] into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that [MATH: \textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,] we get

Content:
[MATH: ∮_(C)F ⋅ nds|= ∮_(C)(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ ((y^{′}(t)i − x^{′}(t)j)/(||r^{′}(t)||))||r^{′}(t)||dt; = ∮_(C)(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ ((y^{′}(t)i − x^{′}(t)j)/(||r^{′}(t)||))||r^{′}(t)||dt; = ∮_(C)(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ (y^{′}(t)i − x^{′}(t)j)dt; = ∮_(C)P(x(t), y(t))y^{′}(t) − Q(x(t), y(t))x^{′}(t)dt; = ∮_(C)Pdy − Qdx.]
